title: Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom
summary: This autobiographical piece from Nelson Mandela's book 'Long Walk to Freedom' describes his inauguration as the first black President of South Africa on 10 May 1994. It paints the grand ceremony in the amphitheatre of the Union Buildings in Pretoria, where the largest gathering of international leaders on South African soil honoured a democracy born out of apartheid. Mandela recalls the two national anthems, the jets trailing the new flag's colours, and his pledge to liberate all people from the chains of poverty and discrimination. He reflects on the twin obligations every man owes to family and country, the meaning of true courage, the learning of hate and love, and how both oppressor and oppressed alike are robbed of their humanity, concluding that freedom is indivisible and must belong to everyone.

Apartheid and the deep wound it created
The twin obligations every man has
Transitory freedoms and basic honourable freedoms

Mandela's idea of the country's greatest wealth
Autobiography as a source: Long Walk to Freedom

sections.heading: About the Author and the Text
sections.para: Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela (1918-2013) was a South African lawyer, freedom fighter and statesman who spent almost three decades in prison for opposing apartheid, the cruel system of racial segregation. After his release he led negotiations that ended white minority rule, and in 1994 he became the first black President of South Africa in the country's first democratic, non-racial elections. He shared the Nobel Peace Prize of 1993 with F. W. de Klerk for the peaceful birth of the new nation. The chapter is an extract from his autobiography 'Long Walk to Freedom', which traces his journey from a village boy to the leader of a free people. His writing is dignified and reflective, mixing personal memory with lessons on courage, forgiveness, duty and equality, and every sentence carries the weight of a man who paid for his ideals with years of his life.
points: Nelson Mandela was born in 1918 and died in 2013, after a life devoted to the freedom of South Africa.
He fought against apartheid, the system of racial segregation that discriminated against non-whites.
He spent nearly thirty years in prison and emerged without bitterness to lead his nation.
In 1993 he received the Nobel Peace Prize jointly with F. W. de Klerk.
The chapter is taken from his autobiography 'Long Walk to Freedom'.
His birthday, 18 July, is celebrated worldwide as Nelson Mandela International Day.
His style blends narration with philosophical reflection on freedom, courage and love.

keyTerms.meaning: A system of racial segregation and discrimination against non-whites in South Africa.
The story of a person's life written by that person, here 'Long Walk to Freedom'.
The formal ceremony of taking office, held on 10 May 1994.
An international award for work towards peace, shared by Mandela and de Klerk in 1993.
Forced separation of people on the basis of race.

sections.trick: Mandela's numbers: 30 years in prison, 1994 first black President, 1993 Nobel Prize, 18 July Mandela Day.
sections.examPointer: Remember that the chapter is an extract from an autobiography; questions on apartheid, the date 10 May 1994 and the idea of courage appear regularly in boards.

sections.heading: The Inauguration Day: 10 May 1994
sections.para: On 10 May 1994 the inauguration of the first democratic, non-racial government of South Africa took place in the amphitheatre of the Union Buildings in Pretoria. It was the largest gathering of international leaders ever seen on South African soil, and the day was bright and clear. Mr F. W. de Klerk was sworn in as second deputy president and Thabo Mbeki as first deputy president, and then Mandela, escorted by his daughter Zenani, took the oath as the first black President of the country, pledging to obey and uphold the Constitution. The highest generals of the defence force and police, who would have arrested him years before, saluted him and pledged their loyalty. Two national anthems were sung, and air force jets trailed smoke in the black, red, green, blue and gold of the new South African flag, a moment Mandela calls a glorious, human rainbow of climate and colours.
points: The date 10 May 1994 is fixed in memory as the day South Africa became a democracy for all races.
The venue was the amphitheatre of the Union Buildings in Pretoria, with leaders from many nations present.
F. W. de Klerk became the second deputy president and Thabo Mbeki the first deputy president.
Mandela was escorted on the historic day by his daughter Zenani.
As President he pledged to obey and uphold the Constitution of the country.
Military generals who would once have arrested him now saluted him and pledged loyalty.
Two national anthems were sung, and jets trailed the colours of the new flag: black, red, green, blue and gold.

keyTerms.meaning: A round building with seats rising in curves, the site of the ceremony.
The body of fundamental laws of a country, which Mandela pledged to uphold.
A solemn promise made on taking office.
The V-shaped trail of smoke in the colours of the new national flag.

sections.trick: 10-5-1994, Pretoria, Zenani beside him; de Klerk second, Mbeki first; two anthems, one new nation.
sections.examPointer: The details of inauguration day are a favourite source of MCQs and extracts; memorise names, the date, the venue and the significance of the two anthems.

sections.heading: Apartheid and the New Nation
sections.para: Mandela reminds us that apartheid was not merely a policy but a deep and lasting wound cut into his country and his people. Under this system the colour of a person's skin decided where he could live, study, work and worship, and the white minority ruled over the black majority without any vote for them. The inauguration of 1994 was therefore much more than the installation of a president: it was the celebration of justice, of the victory of human dignity over racial oppression. Mandela says that never, never and never again would this beautiful land experience the oppression of one by another, and that the sun would never set on so glorious a human achievement. He lets freedom ring from every corner, honouring those who sacrificed so that liberty could belong to blacks and whites alike.
points: Apartheid was a political and social system of racial discrimination against the non-white people of South Africa.
Mandela describes it as a policy that created a deep and lasting wound in his country and his people.
The inauguration was a victory for justice, peace and human dignity, not merely a political change.
Mandela pledged that never again would one people be oppressed by another in that land.
The gathering of world leaders showed that the new South Africa was welcomed and honoured by the world.
The two anthems, Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika and Die Stem, symbolised blacks and whites joining in one nation.

keyTerms.meaning: Cruel and unjust exercise of power over others.
Unfair treatment of people on the basis of race, colour or background.
The worth and honour of every human being, restored in the new nation.
Coming together after conflict; the ceremony united old enemies.

sections.trick: APART-HEID kept people APART; the inauguration of 1994 brought them HEID to heart as one nation.
sections.examPointer: Define apartheid precisely in answers and connect it to the significance of 10 May 1994; examiners reward the link between the wound and the healing.

sections.heading: The Twin Obligations of Every Man
sections.para: Mandela believes that in every country there are times when a man must choose, and that every man has twin obligations: one to his family, to his parents, his wife and his children, and the other to his community, his people and his country. In a free and civil society each man is able to fulfil both obligations and receive credit for his efforts. But in a country like apartheid South Africa it was almost impossible for a man of Mandela's birth and colour to honour both, and a person who tried to serve his people was punished and isolated from his own family, as Mandela himself was. He also speaks of a brief moment when he was free in the boyish sense, running in the fields and swimming, before he learned that his boyhood freedom was an illusion and that his people were not free.
points: Obligation one: to the family, including parents, wife and children, their care and happiness.
Obligation two: to the community, the people and the country, their freedom and welfare.
In a free society a man can honour both obligations and be rewarded for his efforts.
Under apartheid a black man who tried to fulfil his duty to his people was punished and isolated from his family.
Mandela realised his boyhood freedom of running in fields and swimming was only an illusion while his people were enslaved.
As a young man he yearned for the basic honourable freedoms of earning a living, marrying and having a family.
When those freedoms were denied, he understood that his own freedom was incomplete without the freedom of his people.

keyTerms.meaning: The two duties every person owes: to family and to community or country.
Temporary, superficial freedom of youth, an illusion soon broken.
The dignified freedoms of earning one's living, marrying and raising a family.
Separation from family and society, the punishment of activists.

sections.trick: Twin T's: Ties to the family, Ties to the tribe or nation; apartheid punished those who honoured both.
sections.examPointer: The twin obligations are asked as short and long questions; present both duties clearly and show why apartheid made fulfilling them impossible.

sections.heading: Mandela's Idea of True Courage
sections.para: Mandela's most quoted reflection in the chapter is his definition of courage. He says that he learned that courage was not the absence of fear, but the triumph over it, and that the brave man is not he who does not feel afraid, but he who conquers fear. He admits that he was not born with a hunger to be free, nor is anyone; he had moments when he was afraid, but he learned to master them. He pays tribute to the people of South Africa, whose courage he cannot ever fully repay, and to comrades like Oliver Tambo and Walter Sisulu, whom he calls courageous beyond his own standard. For Mandela, freedom was not merely to cast off one's chains, but to live in a way that respects and enhances the freedom of others.
points: Courage is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it.
The brave man is not he who does not feel afraid, but he who conquers fear.
Mandela confesses he had his share of moments of fear and learned to hide his fear behind a mask of bravery.
He regards the people of South Africa as the source of his courage, finer than the purest diamond.
Oliver Tambo and Walter Sisulu are remembered as courageous, wise comrades of the struggle.
True freedom means living in a way that respects and enhances the freedom of others.

keyTerms.meaning: The triumph over fear, not the absence of it.
A fellow member of a movement, sharing struggle and ideals.
An act or statement of respect and admiration.
Symbol of bondage and imprisonment, both literal and social.

sections.trick: Fear Faced is Freedom Gained: courage equals fear conquered, and freedom equals everyone's freedom respected.
sections.examPointer: The definition of courage is a high-frequency 3 and 5 marker; quote the exact line about the brave man who conquers fear.

sections.heading: Oppressor and Oppressed Alike are Robbed
sections.para: One of the most powerful ideas in the chapter is Mandela's insistence that both the oppressor and the oppressed are robbed of their humanity. He knew as well as anyone that the oppressor must be liberated just as surely as the oppressed, because a man who takes away another man's freedom is a prisoner of hatred, locked behind the bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness. The oppressed, on the other hand, carries the burden of indignity and pain. Mandela refused to carry bitterness out of prison: he says that to be free is not merely to cast off one's chains, and that hatred is like chaining oneself. This is why he preached reconciliation, honoured the old regime's generals and shared the ceremony with leaders who once jailed him, believing that liberation must belong to everyone or to no one.
points: The oppressor must be liberated just as surely as the oppressed.
A man who takes away another's freedom is a prisoner of hatred and prejudice.
He is not truly free while he is locked behind the bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness.
The oppressed suffer indignity, humiliation and pain, which rob them of their humanity too.
Mandela chose forgiveness over revenge, honouring even the generals who once served apartheid.
True freedom means living in a way that respects and enhances the freedom of others.

keyTerms.meaning: An unreasonable opinion formed without facts, here racial hatred.
Inability to accept views different from one's own.
Treatment that insults a person's worth and honour.
Restoring friendly relations after conflict.

sections.trick: Both behind bars: the oppressed behind iron bars, the oppressor behind bars of hatred; free both to free all.
sections.examPointer: Explain the paradox that the oppressor also needs liberation; this idea is frequently set as an interpretive 3 or 5 marker.

sections.heading: Learning to Hate, Learning to Love
sections.para: Mandela offers one of the most humane thoughts of the chapter when he says that no one is born hating another person because of the colour of his skin, or his background, or his religion. People must learn to hate, and if they can learn to hate, they can be taught to love, for love comes more naturally to the human heart than its opposite. He admits that even in prison his heart sometimes turned towards hate, but he refused to let hate rule his life, because he knew that hate is like a chain that binds the hater even more tightly than the hated. He ends with the image of man's goodness as a flame that can be hidden but never extinguished, a flame fed by the love, loyalty and courage of ordinary people.
points: Hate is learned behaviour, not natural; children do not hate by birth.
If people can learn to hate, they can be taught to love, because love comes more naturally to the human heart.
Mandela resolved not to let hatred rule his life, even when it was tempting.
Hatred binds the hater in chains as surely as it wounds the hated.
Man's goodness is a flame that can be hidden but never extinguished.
The love and loyalty of the people gave Mandela courage even in the darkest hours.

keyTerms.meaning: The quality of being kind and compassionate to all human beings.
Metaphor for the goodness inherent in every person.
Faithfulness in support of a person, cause or nation.
Complete destruction; hate seeks to obliterate love but fails.

sections.trick: Hate is taught, Love is caught: hate must be learned, but love is the heart's natural lesson.
sections.examPointer: This section supplies famous quotation-based questions; memorise the lines on learning to hate and on the flame of goodness with the word 'extinguished'.

sections.heading: The Country's Greatest Wealth and Mandela's Ideal
sections.para: At the end of the chapter, Mandela turns from ceremony to responsibility. He says that no one is born a president but rather becomes one through struggle, and that he is simply the sum of all those African patriots who had gone before him, men and women of unsurpassed courage and greatness who died for a freedom they never enjoyed. He honours Oliver Tambo and Walter Sisulu as giants of the struggle. When asked what the greatest wealth of his country is, he refuses minerals and jewels and answers that its people are finer than the purest diamond. He repeats the ideal for which he struggled: a democratic and free society in which all persons live together in harmony and with equal opportunities, an ideal he hoped to live for and achieve, but if needs be, an ideal for which he was prepared to die.
points: Mandela calls himself the sum of all African patriots who sacrificed before him.
Oliver Tambo and Walter Sisulu are honoured as geniuses and giants who nurtured the movement.
He remembers comrades who paid with their lives for a freedom they never enjoyed.
Asked about his country's greatest wealth, Mandela answers: its people, finer than the purest diamond.
He renews his ideal of a democratic and free society with harmony and equal opportunities.
He declares that the ideal was one he hoped to live for and achieve, but was prepared to die for if necessary.

keyTerms.meaning: One who loves and serves his country, even at the cost of his life.
Peaceful living together in agreement.
A fair chance for every person to rise, the core of the ideal.
A perfect aim or principle worth living and dying for.

sections.trick: Wealth = PEOPLE: Mandela trades diamonds for people and repeats his ideal: democracy, harmony, equal opportunity.
sections.examPointer: The closing ideal of the chapter is often quoted in long answers on freedom; link it with the oath he took on inauguration day.

sections.heading: Values, Vocabulary and Revision Capsule
sections.para: For revision, hold together three strands: the event, the ideas and the values. The event is the inauguration of 10 May 1994 with its names, anthems and colours. The ideas are the twin obligations, courage as triumph over fear, the liberation of oppressor and oppressed alike, and love as the heart's natural language. The values are forgiveness instead of revenge, dignity for every race, duty to family and country, and faith in the goodness of ordinary people. Alongside these, master the vocabulary that examiners pick: apartheid, amphitheatre, constitution, oppression, discrimination, chevron, transitory and illusions. An answer that quotes one line on courage, names one detail of the ceremony and closes with one value will stand out in any board evaluation of this chapter.
points: Event strand: 10 May 1994, Union Buildings, Pretoria, Zenani, de Klerk, Mbeki, two anthems, jets and flag colours.
Idea strand: twin obligations, courage as triumph over fear, both oppressor and oppressed robbed of humanity.
Value strand: forgiveness, dignity, duty, faith in human goodness.
Vocabulary: apartheid, amphitheatre, constitution, oppression, discrimination, chevron, transitory, illusions.
Remember the source: an extract from the autobiography 'Long Walk to Freedom'.
Remember the date chain: 1993 Nobel Peace Prize, 1994 first black President, 18 July Mandela Day.

keyTerms.meaning: Lasting for a short time only, as boyhood freedoms proved to be.
A false idea or appearance; freedom of the body alone is an illusion.
A V-shaped pattern, describing the jets' coloured smoke.
The act of setting people free from restrictions.

sections.trick: E-I-V for revision: Event 10-5-1994, Idea courage and twin duties, Value forgiveness and dignity.
sections.examPointer: Value-based questions ask what lessons youth can draw from Mandela; answer with forgiveness, courage, duty and equal freedom for all.

boardQuestions.question: When and where was Nelson Mandela sworn in as the first black President of South Africa?
boardQuestions.answer: Nelson Mandela was sworn in as the first black President of South Africa on 10 May 1994, in the amphitheatre of the Union Buildings in Pretoria, before the largest gathering of international leaders ever on South African soil. His daughter Zenani accompanied him, and he pledged to obey and uphold the Constitution of the new democracy.

boardQuestions.question: What was the policy of apartheid? What deep wound did it create?
boardQuestions.answer: Apartheid was the official policy of racial segregation practised in South Africa, under which people were divided and discriminated against on the basis of the colour of their skin, and the white minority ruled over the black majority. Mandela describes it as a system that created a deep and lasting wound in his country and his people. It robbed the black citizens of their land, their votes, their dignity and their basic honourable freedoms such as earning a living and living with family, and it left scars of poverty and humiliation that the new nation of 1994 had to heal.

boardQuestions.question: Why were two national anthems sung on the day of the inauguration? What does this tell us about the new nation?
boardQuestions.answer: On inauguration day two national anthems were sung: Nkosi Sikelel' iAfrika, the anthem of the black people, and Die Stem, the old anthem of the whites. Singing both was a deliberate act of reconciliation, showing that the new South Africa belonged equally to blacks and whites and that the wounds of the past would be healed, not avenged. Mandela himself honoured the military generals who would once have arrested him and shared the ceremony with leaders of the old regime. The twin anthems, like the twin obligations and the two colours of the new flag, announced a nation born of unity, forgiveness and shared hope.

boardQuestions.question: How does Nelson Mandela define courage? Why does he call it the triumph over fear rather than the absence of fear?
boardQuestions.answer: Mandela's definition of courage is one of the finest lessons of the chapter. He says that courage is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it, and explains that the brave man is not he who does not feel afraid, but he who conquers fear. He supports this with honest self-knowledge: he confesses that he was not born with a hunger to be free, that he had his share of moments of fear, and that he learned to hide his fear behind a mask of bravery so that others might feel stronger. Courage, therefore, is not a gift of birth but a habit of the heart, practised again and again. Mandela learned it from the people of South Africa, whose fearless endurance of apartheid he says he can never repay, and from comrades like Oliver Tambo and Walter Sisulu, who stood firm when resistance meant prison or death. The definition matters because it makes courage democratic: any ordinary man or woman can be brave, since bravery does not require the absence of fear, only its mastery. It also explains Mandela's own life: nearly thirty years in prison did not produce a broken man but a leader whose fear had been conquered and converted into strength, forgiveness and the will to free not only the oppressed but also the oppressor who imprisoned them.

boardQuestions.question: What are the twin obligations that every man has, according to Mandela? Why was it impossible to fulfil both under apartheid?
boardQuestions.answer: Mandela believes that in every country and in every life there come moments when a man must choose between two sets of duties, and that every man has twin obligations: the first to his family, to his parents, his wife and his children, and the second to his community, his people and his country. In a free and civil society a man is able to fulfil both obligations and receive credit for his work, raising his family with dignity while serving society openly. But in a country like South Africa under apartheid it was almost impossible for a man of Mandela's birth and colour to honour both. A person who tried to fulfil his duty to his people was automatically punished: he was hounded, isolated from his family, banned from work and, like Mandela himself, thrown into prison for decades. Choosing the family meant betraying the people, and choosing the people meant abandoning the family, so the system broke both duties at once. Mandela chose his people, losing personal freedom for the sake of collective freedom, and this sacrifice makes his reflection deeply moving. The twin obligations also teach students that citizenship is not only private happiness but public responsibility, and that a just society is one in which no one is ever forced to choose between home and country.

boardQuestions.question: 'The oppressor and the oppressed alike are robbed of their humanity.' Explain this statement of Mandela with reference to the chapter.
boardQuestions.answer: This statement contains Mandela's deepest insight into the nature of injustice. It is natural to think that in an unequal system only the victim suffers, but Mandela insists that the oppressor must be liberated just as surely as the oppressed. The oppressor is robbed of his humanity because a man who takes away another man's freedom becomes a prisoner of hatred; he is locked behind the bars of prejudice and narrow-mindedness, and he is not truly free while he fears the very people he oppresses. Every law that humiliates another also coarsens the law-maker; every chain placed on a fellow human being forges a chain around the jailer's own soul. The oppressed, meanwhile, is robbed of humanity through indignity, hunger, separation from family and the daily insult of discrimination, which makes a man feel less than a man. Mandela's genius was to see that apartheid deformed both communities, and that a free South Africa therefore had to liberate both. That is why he walked out of prison preaching reconciliation, saluted the generals of the old regime and invited his former enemies into the government. The statement also carries a universal lesson: freedom is not merely casting off one's own chains but living in a way that respects and enhances the freedom of others, for no one is free while anyone is unfree.

boardQuestions.question: Read the extract and answer the questions: No one is born hating another person because of the colour of his skin, or his background, or his religion. People must learn to hate, and if they can learn to hate, they can be taught to love, for love comes more naturally to the human heart than its opposite. (a) What is the source of hatred according to Mandela? (b) Why is love more natural than hate? (c) What hope does this idea give to a divided society?
boardQuestions.answer: 1) (a) According to Mandela, hatred is not inborn; it is learned from the environment, from education, prejudice and the example of others, and is directed at people because of their colour, background or religion. 2) (b) Love is more natural than hate because it comes more readily to the human heart; Mandela calls man's goodness a flame that can be hidden but never extinguished, so love is the heart's original language and hate only an acquired distortion. 3) (c) This idea gives a divided society the hope that change is possible: since hate had to be taught, it can be untaught, and the very people trained in prejudice can be re-educated in love. 4) Mandela himself proved this by refusing to let bitterness rule his life after nearly thirty years in prison, and by building a rainbow nation with his former enemies. 5) The passage also puts responsibility on educators and parents, for what is taught can be changed by better teaching.

boardQuestions.question: What lessons can students and citizens of today learn from Nelson Mandela's 'Long Walk to Freedom'?
boardQuestions.answer: Mandela's chapter offers lessons that go far beyond one nation's history. First, courage is a habit, not a birthright: we should treat fear as something to be conquered, since the brave man is he who conquers fear. Second, freedom is collective: no one is truly free while his neighbours are unfree, so we must respect and enhance the freedom of others in school, at work and in society. Third, hate is learned and love is natural: we can refuse the lessons of prejudice passed on by our surroundings, because love comes more naturally to the human heart. Fourth, forgiveness is strength, not weakness: Mandela honoured the generals who once would have arrested him and shared power with his old enemies, proving that reconciliation builds nations where revenge destroys them. Finally, duty has two faces: we owe care to our family and service to our community, and a good citizen tries to honour both. A young reader who carries these five lessons forward walks, in a small way, Mandela's long walk to freedom.
